Oil & gas · Zimbabwe

Keep your pipeline reserve clear, and show it with dated maps

The Pipelines Act, as amended in 2026, forbids buildings, structures, trees, wells, boreholes and deep trenches in the pipeline reserve, and any mining or blasting within 125 metres of either side of the pipeline’s centre. We give your integrity and land teams a reviewed register of what stands inside your reserve and that band, with coordinates, distances and the imagery date of each record, and show what has changed since the last survey. Rail and road reserves along the same corridors go into the same register.

Send us your route file See the pipeline sample

The problem, in your words

What the reserve looks like between patrols

“Someone has built in the reserve.”

Homes, sheds, fences and stalls go up where the line runs near a town, a road or a farm. The Act now forbids them, and each one is easier to resolve while it is new and few.

“There is a new trench near the line.”

Wells, boreholes, trenches deeper than 375 mm and new pipes are all barred from the reserve. Fresh digging is where third-party damage starts, and it shows at the surface before anything else does.

“The quarry keeps getting closer.”

No mining or blasting may take place within 125 m of either side of the pipeline’s centre. Pits, spoil heaps and blasted ground move a little with every season, and the band needs watching from both sides.

“The line is being expanded.”

Capacity upgrades, loops and new branches bring contractors, access tracks and new settlement. A dated record from before the works is the one every later discussion goes back to.

Who this is for

  • Pipeline integrity and right-of-way teams
  • Land, wayleave and servitude officers
  • Employees and agents authorised under section 9A
  • Pump-station, depot and terminal managers
  • Engineering and EPC teams on expansions
  • ESIA and RAP consultants
  • Mining and quarry operators beside a pipeline

The 2026 rules in plain words

What may not happen in the reserve, and within 125 m

The Pipelines Amendment Act, 2025 (No. 5 of 2025) was gazetted and came into force on 16 February 2026 (Veritas). Its memorandum says it exists “to ensure maximum protection of the pipelines by prohibiting all activities within the pipeline reserve” (Bill memorandum). The new section 6 of the Pipelines Act [Chapter 13:08] provides (Act No. 5 of 2025):

  • In the reserve (s.6(1)): no one may “erect any building or structure or plant any tree”, or “sink any well or borehole, dig any trench more than three hundred and seventy-five millimetres in depth or lay any pipe”.
  • Within 125 m (s.6(2)): “No person shall conduct any mining or blasting activity within a distance of 125 metres from either side of the centre of the pipeline.”
  • Farming (s.6(3)–(4)): regulations under section 10 may set how far these activities may be allowed in the reserve, and this applies to agricultural activities only.
  • Penalties (s.6(5)–(6)): up to level 10 or six years’ imprisonment, and the court may order the removal of the building, structure, plant or pipe, filling-in, or the end of any digging and ploughing. Damaging a pipeline, pump station, tanks or ancillary works carries up to level 14 or ten years.
  • Inspection (s.9A): the grantee’s authorised employees or agents, and the police, may enter the pipeline servitude, inspect and seize evidence (s.9A(3)–(5)), and the grantee’s employees or agents may order a person to cease any activity pending the grantee’s investigations (s.9A(6)). On private property this needs consent unless an offence is suspected.

Checked 27 September 2026

Read from the amending Act and the Bill’s memorandum. The principal Act was not available to us in full, so we do not publish a reserve width: we measure to the width or polygon you hold. This is a summary, not legal advice.

The Mines and Minerals Act too

Without the pipeline owner’s consent, no prospecting or mining within 25 m of asbestos pipelines over 30 cm in diameter, or 5 m of any other pipeline (s.34(7)). The 2026 rule is wider; how the two interact is for counsel to confirm.

Mining locations in Zimbabwe

Existing pipelines

A register of what stands in the reserve and the 125 m band

We buffer your route in its UTM zone at the reserve width you hold and at 125 m either side of the centre, then list each structure the review confirms, with its distance to the line, its band, its chainage and its coordinates. Cultivated ground and tree cover in the reserve are shown as their own layers; smaller features such as borehole heads are marked only where the imagery shows them clearly.

Inside the 125 m band we map pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and freshly disturbed or blasted ground, each dated to the imagery it first appears on. Around pump stations, tanks and terminals, the line becomes a site boundary, and we list what stands inside it and in a ring around it. Your own facilities are never recorded as encroachment.

Routes are then re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures and new excavations are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and a notice after each survey says what changed and where. A dated record like this is what an inspection under section 9A, a conversation with a landholder or a court case starts from; it supports those processes and never replaces them.

What you receive

  • A reserve register: ID, distance to the line, band, chainage, coordinates
  • Cultivated ground and tree cover in the reserve
  • Pits, spoil and blasted ground within 125 m
  • Structures inside and around pump stations and terminals
  • New and removed structures between surveys
  • A change notice after each survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Expansions and new routes

A baseline before the contractors arrive

A fuel pipeline crosses into Zimbabwe from Mozambique, the 2025 State of the Nation Address announced further upgrades to pipeline capacity (SONA, 28 October 2025), and the Ministry of Energy and Power Development says the Government is interested in extending the network to the southern regions, “such as Bulawayo” (Ministry).

Pipelines are First Schedule projects under the Environmental Management Act and may not be implemented without an EMA certificate (s.97). For a loop, branch or new route we count the structures along each alternative alignment in the same bands, screen slope, drainage crossings and flood-prone ground, and pull the imagery history of contested parcels. Once the route is fixed, a dated register on the cut-off date supports the census and asset inventory, and repeat surveys during construction show new tracks, laydown areas and earthworks.

A corridor that crosses a border is surveyed the same way on both sides: our Mozambique pages cover the 50 m partial protection zone on the Mozambican side.

For expansions

  • Structure counts along alternative alignments
  • Slope, drainage and flood screening
  • A dated register on the cut-off date
  • Construction and earthworks progress between surveys

Rail and road reserves

Where the corridor runs beside a railway or a road

Pipelines, lines and haul roads cross and follow railways and public roads, and each reserve has its own rule. We measure each structure in the same register against the distances that apply to its stretch, from the reserve widths you supply or the defaults in the Acts.

Railways Act, s.38(4)(c)

Railways: 45 m

Anyone who “digs, excavates, drills, tunnels under or otherwise tampers with the ground within forty-five metres on either side of the middle of a railway track”, to the actual or potential detriment of railway safety, faces five to ten years (Railways Act). We flag new excavation in that band.

Roads Act, ss.34, 46

Roads: 31.5 m

Roads are deemed 31.5 m wide unless the Minister gazettes another width, and the road authority may order the removal of a building, structure, fence, ditch or tree that encroaches on a road without written authority (Roads Act).

Roads Act, ss.47–48, 57

Beside the road

No trading within 60 m of a road boundary, or 500 m of an intersection, without permission (s.48); material may not be left within 50 m of a road boundary (s.47); declared restricted roads prohibit structures within their limits (s.57).

Mines and Minerals Act, s.34

Mining beside both

No mining within 45 m of a railway track, including mining buildings, or within 15 m of the middle of a road. New railway routes also need an EMA certificate (Environmental Management Act, First Schedule).

Railway reserve widths and gazetted road widths vary, so we use the widths you supply, and the Roads Act’s 31.5 m only where no other width applies. More on rail and road reserves across Africa.

Drones along a pipeline

Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite shows

Drone surveys are subject to the CAAZ approvals and security clearances each operation requires. Along a pipeline that usually means an operator whose certificate covers the planned flights, the owner’s permission to fly within 30 m of pump stations, tanks and other structures (S.I. 271 of 2018, s.43), approval to fly over, along or within 30 m of a public road (s.44), and legs within sight of the pilot or an observer unless beyond-sight flight is approved (ss.2, 40). Operations adjacent to or above a national key point or strategic installation need CAAZ approval (s.39(3)); we found no public list of key points, and protected-place orders are served on owners rather than published, so your security team is the one that knows. Afridrone is working towards the approvals Zimbabwe requires, and every drone proposal names the company that will fly and its approvals.

If your team already flies the line, send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs: we run the same register and change analysis on them, with a person reviewing every result.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route, the reserve width or polygon, station and valve positions, and say what the register is for: patrol planning, an inspection programme, an expansion or a cut-off date. The bands, imagery and deliverables go into a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures, trees, cultivated ground and excavations are mapped along the whole route from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Look closer where needed

    Your own flights, or drone surveys where the approvals allow, cover the stretches that need detail.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result, each record is measured and banded, and the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, trees, cultivated ground, pits and fresh digging visible from the air
  • Measure each record to the line, the reserve and the 125 m band
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated records that support inspections, engagement and legal processes

What we don’t do

  • Detect leaks, taps, theft or the condition of the pipe
  • See what is under the ground
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Publish a reserve width, carry out land surveys, or decide whether a structure is lawful

Frequently asked questions

How wide is the pipeline reserve in Zimbabwe?

The principal Act was not available to us, so we do not publish a width; we measure to the width or polygon in your servitude records. What the 2026 amendment does fix in the Act is the 125 m band either side of the pipeline’s centre, inside which no mining or blasting may take place (s.6(2)). Both go into the register as bands, with each structure’s distance to the line.

What did the Pipelines Amendment Act, 2025 change?

It rewrote section 6 and added new sections 9A and 10. In force since 16 February 2026, it forbids erecting buildings or structures, planting trees, sinking wells or boreholes, digging trenches deeper than 375 mm and laying pipes in the reserve, and mining or blasting within 125 m of the centre. Penalties rose to level 10 or six years’ imprisonment, from level 4 or three months, and courts can order removal, filling-in or the end of digging and ploughing. Authorised employees or agents of the pipeline’s grantee, and the police, can enter the servitude, inspect and seize evidence; only the grantee’s employees or agents can order an activity to stop, pending the grantee’s investigations.

Can farming continue in the pipeline reserve?

The amended section 6 lets regulations under section 10 set how far activities may be allowed in the reserve, and says that this applies to agricultural activities only. Check with your legal team which regulations apply to your line. Either way, we map cultivated ground in the reserve as its own layer, so the record is there.

Can you detect leaks, taps or theft?

No. Imagery cannot see a leak, a tap, theft or the condition of the pipe. We map what is visible at the surface, such as new structures, fresh digging, spoil, trenches, new tracks and cleared ground, and flag it for your teams to check.

Does the 125 m rule reach quarries and mining locations near our line?

Section 6(2) says that no person shall conduct any mining or blasting activity within 125 m of either side of the centre of the pipeline. The Mines and Minerals Act separately bars mining within 5 m of most pipelines, or 25 m of large asbestos pipelines, without the owner’s consent (s.34(7)); how the two rules interact is a question for counsel. We flag new pits, spoil and blasted ground inside the 125 m band between surveys.

Can you cover the Mozambican section of a cross-border line?

Yes. We survey both sides with the same register format and review steps, measured against each country’s rules: the reserve and the 125 m band in Zimbabwe, and the 50 m partial protection zone in Mozambique. See pipelines in Mozambique.

Send us your pipeline route

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, with pump stations, valves or kilometre posts if you have them, and the reserve width or polygon. Tell us which railways and roads the route runs beside. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
